entries.title: IBS: daily symptoms & food planning
entries.subtitle: Adult symptom patterns, food trials and follow-up
entries.gap: Existing IBS diagnosis summarizes subtypes and treatments; this guide expands practical food trials, symptom history and shared follow-up.

bullets.text: IBS can involve abdominal pain linked to bowel movements, constipation, diarrhea or both. Bloating and a sense of incomplete emptying may also occur.
Symptoms can fluctuate over time. Brain–gut interaction contributes to the disorder; the symptoms are not explained simply by visible intestinal damage.
Describe when pain occurs, how bowel frequency and stool appearance changed, and how long symptoms have been present. These details support clinical assessment.
Include medicines, recent infections, usual foods and family history of celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. Testing depends on the clinical picture.
Rectal bleeding, bloody or black tarry stools, anemia or unexplained weight loss need clinical assessment for conditions beyond IBS.
Blood, stool or other tests may investigate alternative causes. A symptom label alone does not settle the cause of a new change.
Soluble fiber, found in foods such as oats, can help IBS symptoms. The response to diet differs between people.
Increase fiber gradually within the agreed food plan. A rapid increase can worsen gas and bloating; dietitian input can help select changes.
A clinician may recommend a temporary low-FODMAP trial to test whether certain poorly digested carbohydrates contribute to symptoms.
When a trial helps, gradual food reintroduction identifies what can be tolerated. Broad permanent restrictions are not the intended endpoint of that trial.
Activity, sufficient sleep and stress-management approaches can complement the treatment plan. Several approaches may be tried to find what helps.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, gut-directed hypnotherapy or relaxation approaches may be part of care. Medication benefits and unwanted effects belong in follow-up discussions.

entries.title: Constipation: adult bowel routine
entries.subtitle: Assessment, daily habits and when to seek review
entries.gap: Existing opioid and cancer constipation entries are cause-specific; this guide adds a general adult routine and symptom review.

bullets.text: Hard or lumpy stool, painful passage and incomplete emptying can indicate constipation even when the person still passes stool.
Constipation can have several contributors at once, including medicines, reduced activity, intake changes and difficulty emptying the pelvic floor.
Constipation with rectal bleeding, persistent abdominal pain, inability to pass gas, vomiting or fever needs prompt medical assessment.
Unintentional weight loss, persistent symptoms despite self-care or a family history of colorectal cancer warrant clinician review.
Opioids, iron supplements and some anticholinergic medicines can contribute. Include nonprescription products when reviewing potential causes.
Discuss suspected medication effects with the clinician. Changing or stopping a medicine independently can interfere with treatment of the underlying condition.
Regular activity and a predictable time for bowel movements may help. Responding to the urge and allowing enough unhurried time support a routine.
Eating stimulates colon movement; a clinician may suggest trying after breakfast. A footstool may make sitting on the toilet more comfortable.
Introduce fiber gradually with foods such as oats, beans, fruit and vegetables. A dietitian can help set a practical food plan.
Fluids help fiber work and can soften stools. Daily fluid needs depend on health and activity; use the person’s agreed plan rather than a universal volume.
When routine changes are insufficient, a clinician can select further treatment. Laxative choice and duration depend on the individual situation.
Pelvic-floor coordination problems may benefit from biofeedback. Ongoing difficulty emptying deserves evaluation rather than repeated unsupervised treatment changes.

entries.title: Diverticular disease: food & recovery
entries.subtitle: Adult symptom changes, diet progression and follow-up
entries.gap: The diverticulitis diagnosis focuses on acute disease; this guide expands recovery teaching and individualized food planning.

bullets.text: Chronic diverticular symptoms may include bloating, altered bowel habits and lower abdominal discomfort. Similar symptoms can have other causes.
Diverticulitis can cause abdominal pain with fever, chills, nausea or vomiting. Pain may appear suddenly or become worse over several days.
Rectal bleeding needs medical assessment even when the amount seems small. The bleeding source and need for treatment must be evaluated.
Severe illness or complications may require hospital treatment. Failure to improve is a reason for further assessment of the care plan.
A clinician may recommend a short period of clear liquids during diverticulitis, with gradual return to solid food as symptoms improve.
The acute plan differs from longer-term fiber advice. Antibiotics are not required for every episode; treatment is selected for the individual situation.
For chronic symptoms or after an episode, the clinician may suggest more fiber. Introduce changes gradually with a dietitian’s help when needed.
Nutrition Facts labels can help identify fiber-containing choices. The amount and timing should fit the current recovery plan.
Most people with diverticular disease do not need to exclude nuts, seeds or popcorn solely because they have diverticula.
Discuss individual food concerns with the treating team. A higher-fiber pattern with less red meat may lower diverticulitis risk.
Regular physical activity, smoking cessation and weight management when appropriate may lower diverticulitis risk. These are follow-up topics after acute recovery.
Review medicines with the clinician, including NSAIDs, which may increase complication risk. Recurrence planning depends on the person’s history and health.

entries.title: Short bowel: nutrition continuity
entries.subtitle: Adult absorption, hydration and changing support needs
entries.gap: Adds a dedicated adult intestinal-failure support path beyond existing ostomy and parenteral nutrition procedures.

bullets.text: Short bowel syndrome reduces nutrient absorption. Diarrhea, greasy stools, fatigue and weight loss can reflect malabsorption.
Abdominal pain, bloating and gas may accompany intestinal complications. Symptom changes need interpretation with the person’s surgical and disease history.
Reduced or dark urine, marked thirst, dry mouth, dizziness or fainting can signal dehydration. NIDDK advises immediate medical assessment for these symptoms.
Dehydration also involves electrolyte loss. Without treatment it can progress to organ damage or shock.
Nutrition support may include intravenous nutrition, tube feeding and oral intake. The combination depends on intestinal function and the stage of recovery.
Remaining bowel can adapt. As absorption improves, the clinical team may increase enteral or oral intake and reduce parenteral support.
Diet depends on which intestinal segments remain, how well they work, symptoms and the amount of nutrition support already provided.
A dietitian helps balance nutrients, fluids and electrolytes while supporting adaptation. One generic short-bowel diet cannot meet every patient’s needs.
Prescribed oral rehydration solutions contain glucose and electrolytes. Some people also need intravenous fluids; the team adjusts support as absorption changes.
Sugary drinks can worsen dehydration. In selected patients, especially without a colon, excessive low-electrolyte drinks can also worsen losses; drink selection needs individualized advice.
Vitamin or mineral supplements may be needed when parenteral nutrition is reduced. Supplement selection belongs with the treating team.
Persistent intestinal failure may require long-term nutrition support. Its complications and continued need are part of specialist follow-up.

entries.title: Osteoporosis: daily fracture prevention
entries.subtitle: Adult mobility, home safety and ongoing bone care
entries.gap: Adds practical daily fracture prevention to existing screening and postmenopausal disease entries.

bullets.text: Osteoporosis may have no symptoms before a fracture. Hip, spine and wrist fractures are common consequences of reduced bone strength.
Fragile bones can fracture after a minor fall or ordinary stresses. Severe back pain, height loss or a newly stooped posture can accompany vertebral fracture.
Share previous fractures, family history, medicines and illnesses that affect bone health. These details help clinicians assess ongoing risk.
Assessment can include height, posture, strength, gait and balance. Bone-density testing can support diagnosis and treatment monitoring.
Adequate calcium, vitamin D and protein support bone health; poor intake and excessive dieting can increase risk.
Prescribed osteoporosis medicines can help prevent fractures. Nutrition, activity and avoiding smoking remain parts of ongoing care.
An individualized exercise plan can support strength and reduce falls. Discuss safe activity with the clinician or physical therapist.
Physical and occupational therapists can help with function and daily tasks. The plan should reflect existing fractures and physical limitations.
Clear cords and clutter, secure loose rugs and improve lighting. Handrails and bathroom grab bars can make movement safer.
Keep a phone or emergency-call device accessible. A plan for obtaining help after a fall supports safety at home.
Discuss falls, balance problems, vision changes and medicine effects with the care team. These factors can increase fracture risk.
Learning about treatment and involving family or support groups can help people participate in ongoing osteoporosis care.

entries.title: Osteoarthritis: daily function
entries.subtitle: Adult movement, task adaptation and symptom follow-up
entries.gap: Existing diagnosis lists therapies; this guide expands task-level function, equipment and participation in care.

bullets.text: Osteoarthritis affects more than cartilage and can cause pain, swelling and restricted movement. Symptoms and disability differ between people.
Ask how symptoms affect stairs, chair or toilet transfers, walking and gripping objects. These concrete limitations help describe daily burden.
Pain often increases with joint use; advanced disease can also disturb sleep. Short stiffness after inactivity is common.
Fatigue, poor sleep and low mood can accompany the symptom burden. They belong in the discussion of function and quality of life.
History and examination guide evaluation. Blood tests or joint-fluid testing may investigate other causes, including infection or gout.
Early damage may not appear on x-rays. Locking or giving way can prompt additional evaluation rather than assumptions based on prior imaging.
Start activity gradually with professional guidance. A balanced plan may include range of motion, strengthening, balance and low-impact exercise.
Water exercise can reduce joint loading. Weight management, when appropriate, may also reduce stress on weight-bearing joints.
A cane, walker or gripping aid may improve function. Occupational therapy can help protect joints and conserve energy.
Prescribed braces should be fitted by a professional. Reducing repetitive bending and choosing appropriate supports may ease daily tasks.
Follow-up provides a chance to review symptoms and treatment response. Care goals include pain relief, function and participation in daily life.
Education classes and support groups may help with coping. Nurse educators and rehabilitation professionals can support understanding and practical self-management.

entries.title: Gout: daily care & follow-up
entries.subtitle: Adult flare burden, food choices and treatment continuity
entries.gap: Existing gout management emphasizes pharmacology; this guide emphasizes day-to-day coping, comorbidity context and continuity.

bullets.text: Gout can cause sudden severe joint pain, warmth and swelling, often at night. It can affect joints beyond the big toe.
Flares may be separated by symptom-free intervals. Increasing flare frequency or persistent lumps called tophi can indicate a growing disease burden.
High blood urate does not mean everyone will develop gout. Urate buildup and the clinical pattern are distinct parts of the disease picture.
Other conditions can resemble gout. A new or different painful swollen joint needs clinical assessment rather than automatic attribution to a previous diagnosis.
Resting the affected joint and elevating the limb may help reduce flare-related symptoms.
Flare treatment and treatment of the underlying urate burden serve different goals; the clinician individualizes the plan.
Review alcohol, sugar-sweetened drinks and purine-rich animal foods with the care team when planning dietary changes.
Weight management when appropriate and a balanced eating pattern can support broader health as well as gout care.
Diet changes alone are insufficient for frequent flares or tophi. Regular use of prescribed urate-lowering medicine is central to prevention.
A pharmacist or nurse educator can help clarify the treatment plan; discuss proposed medication changes with the clinician.
Kidney disease, kidney stones, hypertension and cardiovascular disease are important associated conditions. Follow-up should account for these alongside joint symptoms.
Diuretics and certain other medicines can increase gout risk. A medication history helps clinicians interpret the overall pattern.

entries.title: Scleroderma: daily support
entries.subtitle: Adult skin, oral care, function and organ follow-up
entries.gap: The systemic-sclerosis diagnosis emphasizes organ therapies; this guide expands oral care, daily function and ongoing symptom communication.

bullets.text: Localized scleroderma mainly affects skin and underlying tissues. Systemic sclerosis can involve blood vessels and internal organs, so follow-up needs differ.
Systemic disease may involve the lungs, heart, kidneys or digestive tract. Skin changes alone do not describe the full scope of care.
Layers, gloves and avoiding cold or wet environments may reduce Raynaud-related symptoms. Moisturizers can help with skin stiffness.
Avoid very hot washing and harsh cleaning products; protect skin during household cleaning. Smoking can worsen vascular symptoms.
Dry mouth and a narrowed mouth opening can complicate hygiene. Regular dental care and adapted brushing or flossing tools may help.
Mouth pain, sores or loose teeth warrant prompt dental contact. Discuss ways to manage dry mouth with dental and medical clinicians.
Small, frequent meals may help digestive symptoms. Swallowing difficulty or poor nutrient absorption requires an individualized diet assessment.
Physical and occupational therapy can support mobility and daily activities, including hand and jaw function.
Report new breathlessness, dry cough, unusual fatigue or swollen feet. Lung testing can detect problems before symptoms become obvious.
Follow the blood-pressure monitoring plan. A reading higher than usual or new headache or breathlessness needs prompt clinician contact because renal crisis can be serious.
Treatment aims to limit progression and relieve symptoms. Ongoing monitoring matters even when the visible skin findings are stable.
The range of possible organ involvement makes a shared account of current symptoms and affected systems useful across follow-up care.

targetedCorrections.old: Do NOT start ULT during acute attack (worsens). Continue ULT if patient already on it.
targetedCorrections.new: Flare control and long-term urate reduction have different goals. The clinician individualizes medication selection and timing.

targetedCorrections.old: URATE-LOWERING THERAPY (ULT) — start 2–4 weeks after acute attack resolves (or sooner if frequent attacks/tophi/CKD): allopurinol first-line; titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL (<5 with tophi).
targetedCorrections.new: For frequent flares or tophi, lifestyle measures alone are insufficient; regular prescribed urate-lowering treatment helps prevent further flares and reduce tophi.

targetedCorrections.old: No systemic features (no fever, no fatigue) — important distinction from inflammatory arthritis.
targetedCorrections.new: Pain and functional limitations may be accompanied by fatigue, sleep difficulty or depressed mood; these effects deserve assessment.

reviewNotes: Proposed tiers require independent clinical assessment. Tier A: short-bowel support and systemic sclerosis because of fluid/organ risk. Remaining six guides proposed Tier B.
NIDDK IBS/constipation source dates are 2017/2018; stable education only, no drug algorithms or supplement endorsements.
New content uses specific source pages. Older linked entries are not newly approved by navigation membership.
The manifest records workflow state and is not an application publication gate.
ACR 2020 guideline primary text confirmed the legacy blanket ban on starting urate-lowering therapy during a flare was inappropriate; replacement statements use NIAMS public-domain prose.
No dosing protocols, pediatric instructions, copyrighted images or proprietary instruments added.
